passage:
I've been thinking about why I lied about Pallavi's birthday party. I told Mummy it was a study group. The truth is, I knew what she'd say if I asked: "No. Too late. Who are these people?" She's said it every time since Class 8. So I didn't ask. I just wanted one normal evening, like everyone else gets, laughing and eating cake. Now she's found out, and I feel terrible when I see her face. But I also feel angry. Would she have said yes if I'd been honest? Never. In our house, the truth just gets you a quicker no. Being a daughter here means choosing between lying and missing everything.
— Himani

qa.q: What did Himani tell Mummy the party was?
qa.a: She told Mummy it was a study group.

qa.q: What does Himani feel now that Mummy has found out?
qa.a: She feels terrible when she sees Mummy's face, but also angry, believing honesty would only have got her a quicker no.

qa.q: What could help Himani and Mummy at this stage?
qa.a: Himani could tell Mummy the real reason, that she expected a flat no, so they can talk about making it safe to ask.

qa.q: How might Mummy see the lie differently if she heard Himani's reason?
qa.a: Mummy might still be hurt but could see that her automatic "no" made honesty feel pointless to Himani.

grounding: Shows a teen girl who lied because she expected a flat no, feeling both guilt and resentment and believing honesty was never safe at home.

passage:
School counsellor's note, 22 July. Student: Arohi, Class 11.
Arohi came in after her father, Mr Kamal Verma, discovered she had gone to a friend's concert while saying she was at the library. She was defensive at first, arms crossed. Then she said, "If I'd asked, Papa would've said no before I finished the sentence. He always does." She said she wanted one evening where she felt like a normal teenager. She admitted feeling guilty, "especially when he looked so hurt." But she also said, quietly, "Being honest has never worked in our house." Her eyes filled as she said it. Next step: with her permission, a joint session with her father on how she can ask and how he can listen.

qa.q: Where did Arohi say she was?
qa.a: She said she was at the library.

qa.q: What does Arohi believe about honesty at home?
qa.a: She feels sad and hopeless about it, believing honesty has never worked in their house because her father says no before she finishes asking.

qa.q: What next step does the counsellor plan, and why does it help?
qa.a: A joint session with her father, with her permission, so they can work on how she asks and how he listens.

qa.q: How did Mr Kamal Verma seem to feel about the lie, according to Arohi?
qa.a: He looked very hurt, which made Arohi feel especially guilty.

grounding: Shows a teen girl who lied to get a normal evening out because she expected a refusal, feeling guilt and resentment about honesty never being safe.

passage:
Rukmini sat on her bed in their Andheri flat, the door shut. Through it she could hear her father, Darshan, still talking to her mother in a low, hard voice.
She had lied. She'd said she was at a group study and gone to Isha's birthday at a café instead. She felt sick about it.
But she also felt angry. If she'd asked, Papa would have said no in two seconds. He always did. "Too late." "Not with those friends." "Study first." She had just wanted one normal evening, like everyone else.
She hugged her knees. She was sorry. But she wasn't sure honesty had ever actually worked in this house.

qa.q: Where did Rukmini actually go?
qa.a: To Isha's birthday at a café.

qa.q: What was Rukmini feeling as she sat on her bed?
qa.a: She felt guilty and sick about lying, but also resentful, believing her father always said no.

qa.q: What turning point is available at this stage?
qa.a: Rukmini could explain to her parents why she lied, that she expected a flat no, and they could listen and think about how to make asking feel safer.

qa.q: What might Darshan be experiencing right now?
qa.a: He is likely hurt and angry about the lie, and perhaps worried about where she was.

grounding: A teenage girl lied because she expected a flat no and wanted a normal evening, and feels both guilt and resentment that honesty never felt safe.

passage:
"Why did you lie to me, Gurpreet?" asked Mummy.
"Because you'd have said no."
"You don't know that."
"I do! You always say no. Last time I asked about the fair, you said no. The time before, the movie, no."
"That doesn't make lying okay."
"I know." Gurpreet's voice cracked. "I feel terrible. But I just wanted one evening. Like a normal girl."
Gargi, her little sister, peeped in from the doorway.
"Go to your room, Gargi," said Mummy.
Gurpreet looked at the floor. "You never let me tell you the truth," she said, very quietly. "You just say no before I finish."

qa.q: What had Mummy said no to last time?
qa.a: The fair, and before that the movie.

qa.q: What was Gurpreet feeling when her voice cracked?
qa.a: She felt guilty and terrible about lying, but also resentful that her mother always said no before she finished.

qa.q: What turning point is available to Mummy now?
qa.a: Mummy could stop and ask Gurpreet to finish what she wants to say, listening to why she felt she couldn't ask.

qa.q: What is Mummy experiencing during this conversation?
qa.a: She is hurt and angry about the lie, and may be surprised to hear that Gurpreet feels she is never allowed to tell the truth.

grounding: A teenage girl explains she lied because she expected a flat no, feeling guilt and resentment that honesty has never felt safe at home.

passage:
I remember lying on the floor of my room after Harsha bhaiya found out. He'd seen me at the mall when I'd said I was at Sneha's for a project.
He didn't tell Mummy. He just asked me, "Why?"
And I didn't know how to say it. Because asking was pointless. Because in our house, "Can I go?" always meant a lecture and a no. Because I just wanted to eat fries with my friends like a normal fourteen-year-old girl.
I felt so guilty I couldn't eat dinner. But I was angry too, at them, at me, at the whole house where honesty never seemed to work.
I'm Shreya. That's the first time I understood why I lied.

qa.q: Where did Shreya say she was?
qa.a: At Sneha's for a project.

qa.q: What was Shreya feeling that evening?
qa.a: Shreya felt guilty, unable to eat dinner, and also angry and resentful at a home where honesty never seemed to work.

qa.q: What turning point did Harsha bhaiya create?
qa.a: By asking "Why?" instead of telling their mother, he gave Shreya a chance to understand and name the real reason she lied.

qa.q: What might Harsha bhaiya have been experiencing?
qa.a: He was probably worried and disappointed, but also curious and wanting to understand his sister rather than punish her.

grounding: A teenage girl recalls lying because she expected a flat no and wanted a normal evening, feeling guilt alongside resentment about her home.

passage:
School counsellor's note, Class 10, Friday. Written by Thomas, counsellor.

Amandeep came in after her mother found out she'd lied about a study group and gone to a friend's birthday instead. She sat with her arms folded for ten minutes.

Then she said, "If I'd asked, it would've been no. It's always no. I just wanted one normal evening." She said she felt bad about the lie, "really bad," but also angry that honesty "never worked in our house anyway."

I noted both feelings sitting side by side: guilt and resentment. I didn't argue with either. I asked her to tell me about a time she'd been honest and what happened. She described asking for a sleepover in Class 8 and being lectured for an hour.

Next step: with her agreement, a joint session with her mother next week, to talk about why asking feels unsafe.

qa.q: What did Amandeep lie about?
qa.a: She lied about a study group and went to a friend's birthday instead.

qa.q: What was Amandeep feeling about the lie?
qa.a: She felt guilty, 'really bad', but also resentful and angry, believing honesty had never been safe at home.

qa.q: Why is a joint session a wise next step?
qa.a: It lets Amandeep and her mother talk about why asking feels unsafe, so the reason behind the lie can be addressed, not only the lie.

qa.q: How might Amandeep's mother see the lie right now?
qa.a: Her mother likely feels hurt and betrayed, and may not yet know that Amandeep expected a flat no.

grounding: A counsellor's note shows a teen who lied expecting a flat no, feeling both guilt and resentment because honesty never felt safe.
